questions.question: What does the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix actually do to an environment variable?
options: It encrypts the value before sending it to the browser
It inlines the value into the client-side JavaScript bundle, making it readable by anyone who opens dev tools
It restricts the variable to server-only code
It has no effect unless combined with another flag
questions.explanation: NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables are bundled into client JS at build time — the prefix means 'exposed to the browser,' not 'protected.'

questions.question: Why is it safe for this app to expose NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY to the browser?
options: Because the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix encrypts it
Because Supabase's anon key is designed to be public, and real data protection comes from Row Level Security policies enforced at the database
Because it expires after 24 hours automatically
It isn't actually safe and should be changed
questions.explanation: The anon key only identifies the project; RLS policies on the database are what actually restrict which rows a request can read or write.

questions.question: How does Next.js protect Server Actions from cross-site request forgery (CSRF) by default?
options: It doesn't — you must implement CSRF tokens manually
It checks that the request's Origin header matches the deployment's own host before executing the action
It requires every Server Action to be behind a login
It encrypts all form data automatically
questions.explanation: Next.js verifies the Origin header matches the app's own host, rejecting cross-origin Server Action calls before the action code runs — no manual token needed.

questions.question: Does Server Actions' built-in CSRF protection mean you can skip validating/sanitizing the submitted data itself?
options: Yes, CSRF protection covers all input safety concerns
No — CSRF protection only verifies the request's origin; the content still needs validation (shape/length, parameterized queries) and sanitization before being rendered as HTML
Only if the user is logged in
Yes, as long as NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables aren't involved
questions.explanation: CSRF protection is about who can call the action; it says nothing about whether the submitted content is safe to store or render, which remains the developer's responsibility.
